title: Preparation, Instrument, Course, Cabinet: institutional teaching ecologies of nineteenth-century microscopy
research_problem: Histories of microscopy often foreground instruments, methods, or disciplinary ideas separately. The source registry now exposes institutions in which preparations, microscopes, course records, catalogues, storage systems and publications can be reconstructed as coordinated teaching infrastructures.
working_claim: Practical microscopy was institutionally produced through different documentary and material ecologies. A preparation became teachable when it was made or acquired, entered an inventory or catalogue, could be located, was coordinated with an instrument and course sequence, and could survive repeated handling. These systems varied sharply by institution; a global history therefore need not be organized as a simple diffusion of microscope technology from one centre to another.

research_payoff.first_order_argument: The teaching history of microscope slides can be written as the coordination of preparations, instruments, courses and retrieval systems. The same practical technology generated different institutional documentary forms: ledgers in Tokyo, a published apparatus/preparation catalogue in Coimbra, surviving slide-apparatus chains in Cambridge, and card-catalogued serial anatomy at Harvard.
research_payoff.anti_diffusion_guard: Geographic comparison should not be framed as Britain/Europe inventing a standardized system that other institutions simply received. The comparandum is how each institution made preparations reproducibly locatable and usable for practical teaching.
